evidence_quotes.quote: Based on survey data of 202 street children who were purposively sampled, the findings revealed that street children lack access to food, education, accommodation, health care and proper sanitation.

The goal of this study was to assess the well-being of street children to see if alternative mechanisms and strategies could be implemented by the government of Zimbabwe to enhance the living standards of street children.
A survey questionnaire was used to gather quantitative data from 202 street children aged between 6 and 18 years who took part in this study.

Table 2 above reported that 71.3% of street children do not have access to toilets. Furthermore, 69.8% reported not having access to bathing facilities. In addition, 65.3% do not have access to water.

These findings are congruent with those of Maepa (2018), who claimed that corruption, lack of efficiency, poor management of finances and bureaucracy in public state entities severely affect street children, who lack access to safe drinking water and public restrooms.

criterion_notes.c1: Satisfied descriptively: although the study is a broad developmental social work assessment of street children's holistic well-being, Theme 2 (Physical risks, Table 2 on PDF p. 14) specifically measures and reports street children's access to toilets, bathing facilities, and water.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the empirical survey examines general living conditions and risks in the street environment (demographics, livelihoods, sleeping locations, food sources, ailments, sanitation access, criminal offences, antisocial behaviour, and school dropout) using univariate frequency distributions; it does not measure or empirically analyse any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor in relation to water or sanitation access. Background discussion of social welfare programmes (DSD), a passing reference to municipal by-laws prohibiting street vending/begging, and a secondary citation in the Discussion to Maepa (2018) on public-sector corruption and bureaucracy are not empirical analyses of governance factors in this study. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, no rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariffs, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure) is examined.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfied: primary quantitative empirical study administering a semi-structured survey questionnaire to 202 purposively sampled street children in Harare Metropolitan Province, analysed via descriptive frequency statistics in SPSS.
criterion_notes.c4: Satisfied: Table 2 (PDF p. 14) reports binary self-reported access outcomes for toilets (71.3% without access), bathing facilities (69.8% without access), and water (65.3% without access) among the 202 surveyed street children.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfied for study reporting completeness: the population and unit of analysis (202 individual street children aged 6-18 in Harare), general environmental condition (living/working in the urban street environment), outcomes (including self-reported water and sanitation access), and study design (cross-sectional descriptive survey) are clearly identifiable, though no legal or governance exposure is examined.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfied: full text is published in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional quantitative descriptive survey using a semi-structured questionnaire
population_and_sample: 202 purposively sampled street children aged 6 to 18 years in Harare Metropolitan Province, Zimbabwe (unit of analysis: individual child)
exposure: Living or working in the urban street environment (no legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor empirically examined)
outcome: Self-reported access (Yes/No) to toilets, bathing facilities, water, and a clean environment (Table 2), alongside broader well-being indicators (livelihoods, accommodation, food access, ailments, criminal offences, antisocial behaviour, and school dropout)
rationale: Exclude (E03 - Wrong exposure). Although this quantitative cross-sectional survey of 202 street children in Harare reports descriptive statistics on lack of access to toilets (71.3%), bathing facilities (69.8%), and water (65.3%) as part of a broad social-work assessment of child well-being, it does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor governing water or sanitation service access under either the plain wording or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. The study reports univariate frequencies describing street living conditions, and its only link between public-sector bureaucracy/governance and water or restroom access is a secondary citation to Maepa (2018) in the Discussion.
